sec.title: Purpose:
sec.p: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has been a breakthrough in many hematologic malignancies, but success in relapsed/refractory (R/R) acute myeloid leukemia (AML) has been limited due to underwhelming response rates and high on-target/off-tumor toxicity. This phase 1 dose-escalation trial evaluated the safety and efficacy of KITE-222, an autologous CAR T-cell therapy that recognizes C-type lectin-like molecule 1 (CLL-1), predominantly expressed on myeloid cells but absent on normal hematopoietic stem cells and other tissues.

sec.title: Patients and Methods:
sec.p: Patients with R/R AML (≥50 kg) received a single intravenous infusion of 3 × 107 (cohort 1), 1 × 108 (cohort 2), or 3 × 108 (cohort 3) KITE-222 CAR+ T cells. The primary endpoint was the incidence of dose-limiting toxicities (DLT). Key secondary endpoints included overall remission rate, incidence of adverse events (AE), and pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics.

sec.title: Results:
sec.p: Twelve patients received KITE-222. One patient in cohort 3, who was the only patient to receive two courses of lymphodepleting chemotherapy, experienced a DLT (prolonged grade 4 neutropenia/thrombocytopenia) but achieved a best response of morphologic leukemia-free state on day 14 following infusion (confirmed on day 44). All patients experienced grade ≥3 AEs, none had grade ≥3 cytokine release syndrome, and one had grade ≥3 immune effector cell–associated neurotoxicity syndrome. Clinically meaningful responses were lacking across dose levels despite detectable CAR T-cell expansion. Although two of five cohort 3 patients with clear expansion had near-complete depletion of CLL-1+ bone marrow blasts after infusion, CLL-1− blasts persisted, and reductions in total blasts were not observed.

sec.title: Conclusions:
sec.p: Despite successful manufacturing and acceptable safety, KITE-222 lacked preliminary efficacy, warranting future studies that address CLL-1 heterogeneity and focus on improving in vivo expansion and antitumor activity.

boxed-text.p: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has proven successful in multiple hematologic malignancies; however, the benefit in relapsed/refractory acute myeloid leukemia (AML) has been limited due to underwhelming responses and high on-target/off-tumor toxicity. CD33 and CD123 were previously evaluated as CAR targets, but expression on normal hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPC) and the likelihood of high-grade, therapy-induced cytopenias have challenged development. C-type lectin-like molecule 1 (CLL-1), predominantly expressed on myeloid cells but absent on normal HSPCs and other tissues, is a promising CAR target. This phase 1 dose-escalation trial evaluated the safety and efficacy of KITE-222, an autologous CLL-1–directed CAR. One patient experienced a dose-limiting toxicity yet achieved a best response of morphologic leukemia-free state. Despite successful manufacturing of KITE-222 products for all patients, responses were lacking due to heterogeneous CLL-1+ blast populations and absent, minimal, or highly variable CAR T-cell expansion. Future studies aimed at improving in vivo expansion and antitumor effects of CAR T cells in AML are needed.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is an aggressive disease with limited improvements in the 5-year survival rate despite recent advances and approvals of targeted therapies (1–4). In the United States, AML accounts for the largest number of annual deaths from leukemias, with an estimated 5-year relative survival rate of approximately 33% among newly diagnosed patients with AML [from 2016 to 2022] (3, 4).

Patients with relapsed/refractory (R/R) AML face poor outcomes (5). Despite initial response to induction therapy, relapse rates for AML vary from ∼30% to 35% in younger patients (e.g., <60 years old) with favorable risk to ∼70% to 80% in patients with adverse risk who are older (5). Moreover, ∼10% to 40% of patients do not respond to first-line intensive induction therapy, and outcomes of salvage chemotherapy in such primary refractory AML are dismal (1, 6, 7). Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant (allo-HSCT) is the only potentially curative option for patients with R/R disease but typically requires that patients be in remission prior to undergoing transplant (8–10). Although not all patients are eligible for allo-HSCT and treatment-related morbidity and mortality remain an issue, improvements in technique and risk stratification have led to higher transplant numbers and more favorable outcomes in certain patient subsets (8–11). Nonetheless, patients with R/R AML continue to have poor overall survival and remain a population with significant unmet need (12–14).

Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapies have revolutionized the treatment of several B-cell–based hematologic malignancies, particularly lymphoma, acute lymphoblastic leukemia, and multiple myeloma, but success to date has been limited in AML, with underwhelming response rates and high on-target/off-tumor toxicity across multiple targets and constructs (1, 15–17). Toxic effects on the healthy hematopoietic compartment and intratumoral and interpatient heterogeneity in the expression of target antigens have been barriers to developing effective CAR T-cell therapies in AML (1, 8, 15, 18). CD33 and CD123 have been evaluated as target antigens due to high and frequent expression across different AML genotypes, but the expression of these antigens on normal hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPC) and the likelihood of high-grade cytopenias resulting from CAR T-cell therapy have challenged clinical development (18).

C-type lectin-like molecule 1 (CLL-1; also known as CLEC12A or CD371), a type II transmembrane glycoprotein, is a promising target antigen for CAR T-cell therapy in AML, given that expression is restricted to myeloid cells, with minimal to no expression on normal HSPCs and no expression in other tissues (19–21). The depletion of normal granulocytes, monocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells during CLL-1–directed CAR T-cell therapy due to CLL-1 expression by such normally differentiated myeloid cells may be a manageable risk that can be partially overcome by the preservation of CLL-1–negative HSPCs (20–22). In patients with AML, CLL-1 expression has been documented across many histologic subtypes, with 78% to 92% of tumors testing positive at diagnosis (positivity defined by CLL-1 presence on >20% of blasts; refs. 8, 19, 21, 22).

KITE-222 is an autologous CAR T-cell therapy comprising positively selected CD4+ and CD8+ T cells genetically modified to express a CD28 costimulatory domain–containing CAR that recognizes endogenous CLL-1. Here, we report results from a phase 1 multicenter dose-escalation trial of KITE-222 in adult patients with R/R AML.

sec.title: Patients and study design
sec.p: This was a phase 1, open-label trial (NCT04789408) to evaluate the safety and efficacy of KITE-222 in adult patients with R/R AML. Eligible patients were ≥18 years old, with R/R de novo or secondary AML [as defined by the European Leukemia Network (ELN) 2017 classification; ref. 23]. Additional inclusion criteria were morphologic disease in the bone marrow (BM; ≥5% blasts) and/or peripheral blood (PB) within 28 days of enrollment, prior exposure to an FDA-approved targeted therapy for patients with a targetable mutation (i.e., IDH1, IDH2, or FLT3), adequate renal, hepatic, pulmonary, and cardiac function, and an absolute lymphocyte count (ALC) ≥100 cells/μL. CLL-1–positive disease was not required for enrollment. Patients with prior CLL-1–directed therapy or genetically modified T-cell therapy were excluded. Patients were required to meet institutional criteria for allo-HSCT fitness and have a stem cell donor identified and readily available for a potential allo-HSCT following therapy with KITE-222. Patients with active central nervous system (CNS) disease involvement were excluded. Full eligibility criteria are provided in Supplementary Methods S1.

This study of KITE-222 was conducted in accordance with recognized international scientific and ethical standards, including the International Council for Harmonisation guideline for Good Clinical Practice and the ethical principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. The study protocol and all amendments were approved by the Institutional Review Board at each participating site. Written informed consent/assent for participation was obtained from all patients.

The study design included dose-escalation cohorts and an expansion cohort to be informed by the dose-escalation results (Supplementary Fig. S1). In the dose-escalation portion, three dose-level cohorts were assessed using a 3 + 3 study design to determine the maximum tolerated dose. For patients ≥50 kg, KITE-222 was administered as a flat dose of 3 × 107 (cohort 1), 1 × 108 (cohort 2), and 3 × 108 (cohort 3) CAR+ T cells. The dose was reduced by one third of the target dose (rounded to the nearest 10 million cells) for patients <50 kg. Further details of the dose-escalation design are provided in Supplementary Methods S1.

sec.title: Treatments and procedures
sec.p: Eligible patients underwent leukapheresis to obtain T cells for the manufacture of KITE-222 using fresh apheresis material at the sponsor’s facility. Patients received lymphodepleting chemotherapy (LDC) with cyclophosphamide 300 mg/m2/day intravenously and fludarabine 30 mg/m2/day intravenously on days −5, −4, and −3 prior to KITE-222 infusion. Based on limited CAR T-cell expansion observed after infusion in patients who had high numbers of circulating blasts (including patients in cohorts 1 and 2 and the first patient in cohort 3), and in consideration of the possible inverse relationship between tumor burden and in vivo CAR T-cell expansion seen in other leukemias (24), the study protocol was amended following a review of the safety and translational data with the investigators and safety review team. With the amendment, the cyclophosphamide dosage was increased to 750 mg/m2/day for the last five patients enrolled in cohort 3. Optional bridging therapies that (after protocol amendments) included hydroxyurea, intermediate-/low-dose cytarabine, or venetoclax–azacitidine regimens were administered between leukapheresis and lymphodepletion at the investigator’s discretion. Bridging therapy was highly recommended for patients with high tumor burden defined by high BM involvement (>30% leukemic blasts at screening) or high PB counts [>1,000 blasts/mm3 or >5,000 white blood cells (WBC)/mm3 at leukapheresis].

KITE-222 (delivered to treatment centers as a frozen product) was administered as a single intravenous infusion (day 0), and patients remained hospitalized for at least 14 days after infusion to monitor for cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and immune effector cell–associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS). After day 28, conditioning chemotherapy for allo-HSCT could begin, at the investigator’s discretion, for the consolidation of response in patients treated with KITE-222 or for the rescue of non–leukemia-related prolonged cytopenias before day 42.

sec.title: Endpoints and assessments
sec.p: The primary endpoint was the incidence of dose-limiting toxicities (DLT). Secondary endpoints included overall remission rate, incidence of adverse events (AE), pharmacokinetics (PK), and pharmacodynamics (PD).

AEs were graded using the NCI Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (version 5.0). DLTs were defined as specific KITE-222–related nonhematologic events occurring within 28 days after KITE-222 infusion (described in Supplementary Methods S1) or ongoing grade 4 neutropenia or thrombocytopenia (that was not due to leukemia persistence) at day 42 if allo-HSCT conditioning therapy had not been initiated by that time. CRS and ICANS were graded per the American Society for Transplantation and Cellular Therapy consensus grading proposed by Lee and colleagues (25).

Overall responses were based on investigator assessment per ELN 2017 classification (23), with BM monitoring required at day 14 (±2 days) and day 28 (±3 days) following KITE-222 infusion and follow-up assessments performed at day 42 (±3 days) and month 3 (±1 week) per protocol. PK assessments of transduced anti–CLL-1 CAR T cells in PB were performed by PCR. T-cell product phenotypes were characterized by flow cytometry. PD analyses included the measurement of key serum analytes using validated immunoassays and the measurement of CLL-1+ blasts in PB and BM. CLL-1 expression on blasts was quantified using validated multiparameter flow cytometry assays and standardized fluorescent beads to calculate antigen density per cell. Detailed methods for PK and PD analyses are included in Supplementary Methods S1.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: The safety analysis set included all patients treated with any dose of KITE-222. The DLT-evaluable set included all patients treated with KITE-222 in each dose-escalation cohort at the target dose level for that cohort and who were followed for ≥28 days after infusion. The full criteria for the DLT-evaluable population are provided in Supplementary Methods S1. A formal hypothesis was not tested, and summary statistics and reported P values are descriptive.

sec.title: Study population
sec.p: Between July 2021 and November 2023, 15 patients from study sites in the United States and France were enrolled in the trial and underwent leukapheresis. Eighty percent of enrolled patients (12/15) were ultimately treated with KITE-222 (Fig. 1; Supplementary Table S1). The data cutoff date for this analysis was May 18, 2024.

Twelve patients received KITE-222 in three progressive dose-escalation cohorts (cohorts 1 and 2, n = 3 each; cohort 3, n = 6). One patient did not start LDC due to a lung infection, and two patients were not treated with KITE-222 after LDC due to a COVID infection (n = 1) or a subdural hematoma (n = 1). Following a protocol amendment, five patients in cohort 3 received a higher LDC dosage that led to an increased cumulative target cyclophosphamide dose of 2,250 mg/m2 per patient versus 900 mg/m2 in the other patients. Six patients received one or more bridging therapies after leukapheresis, including hydroxyurea (n = 2), cytarabine (n = 5), or venetoclax with azacitidine (n = 3).

KITE-222 was successfully manufactured and delivered to the study site for all 15 enrolled patients, with products meeting all predefined quality control criteria for 13 patients. Two patients (one each in cohorts 2 and 3) had products that were out of specification but met the dose-level requirement (following discussions between investigators and the medical monitor, an FDA exemption was granted, and both patients received KITE-222). KITE-222 product characteristics are summarized in Supplementary Table S2. The median time from leukapheresis to KITE-222 product release was 14 days (range, 11–21), and the median time from leukapheresis to infusion was 28.5 days (range, 19–56).

Among patients treated with KITE-222 (N = 12), the median age was 57.5 years (range, 31–76), 67% were White, and 58% were male (Table 1; representativeness of study participants is described in Supplementary Table S3). Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0 and 1 was reported in 25% and 75% of patients, respectively. Patients had received a median of three prior lines of AML therapy (range, 1–6), and 50% had received prior allo-HSCT. Additional baseline characteristics, including AML-associated genetic abnormalities, are included in Table 1.

sec.p: At baseline (defined as the last nonmissing value measured prior to LDC), median ALC and WBC counts were 0.575 × 109 cells/L (range, 0.2–1.23) and 1.3 × 109 cells/L (range, 0.4–16.7), respectively. Median platelet count at lymphodepletion was 23.5 × 109 cells/L (range, 5–58). Median percentages of total blasts at baseline measured by the investigator per morphologic assessment were 31% (range, 5%–88%) in the BM (n = 11) and 6% (range, 0%–97%) in PB (Table 1). Median percentages of CLL-1+ blasts by flow cytometry, expressed as a percentage of total blasts, were 31.2% (range, 6.4%–94.4%) in the BM (n = 11) and 51% (range, 0%–100%) in PB per central assessment. The distribution of CLL-1+ blast percentages at baseline across the 12 treated patients is shown in Supplementary Table S4. At baseline, 64% (7/11) of treated patients with available CLL-1 expression data presented with >20% CLL-1 positivity of BM blasts, a historical threshold that has been arbitrarily considered “positive” for antigen expression (19, 21, 26).

Median follow-up, defined as the time from KITE-222 infusion to the last date known alive, was 3.2 months (range, 0.9–12.3). The trial was terminated after enrollment for cohort 3 due to a lack of preliminary efficacy, and the expansion phase was not initiated.

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: Of the 12 patients treated with KITE-222, 11 were evaluable for DLTs (primary endpoint analysis); one patient (cohort 3) died due to disease progression prior to the minimum follow-up duration of ≥28 days after KITE-222 infusion that was required for inclusion in the DLT-evaluable set.

A patient in cohort 3 who achieved morphologic leukemia-free state (MLFS; described in the Efficacy section) experienced one DLT comprising prolonged grade 4 neutropenia and thrombocytopenia that were ongoing after day 42 and were both considered related to LDC and KITE-222 treatment. This patient received two rounds of LDC, each at the target dose of cyclophosphamide (750 mg/m2 × 3 days) and fludarabine (30 mg/m2 × 3 days), as required per protocol owing to a delay in KITE-222 infusion of >2 weeks (due to infection) after receiving the initial LDC. The patient also experienced grade 2 CRS on day 2 that resolved on day 3 and grade 2 hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) on day 25 that was still ongoing at the time of death (due to LDC-related sepsis) on day 52; both CRS and HLH were considered related to KITE-222 treatment. Additional patient details, including prior treatment history, genomic profile, and clinical course of HLH related to KITE-222 treatment, are provided in Supplementary Results S1.

All 12 patients experienced any-grade and grade ≥3 treatment-emergent AEs (TEAE; Table 2). Grade ≥3 TEAEs reported in >1 patient were cytopenias (58%), infection (50%), febrile neutropenia (42%), decreased lymphocyte count (33%), sepsis (25%), decreased WBC count (17%), pneumonia (17%), pyrexia (17%), and device-related infection (17%). Nine patients (75%) had grade ≥3 serious AEs. The most common KITE-222–related grade 3 to 4 TEAE was pyrexia [2/12 infused patients (17%), Supplementary Table S5]. There were no KITE-222–related grade 5 TEAEs. Supplementary Table S6 shows the concentrations of leukocytes, lymphocytes, monocytes, and neutrophils before and after LDC and at serial time points after KITE-222 infusion for each of the 12 patients.

sec.p: Nine patients (75%) experienced grade ≤2 CRS; no patients had grade ≥3 CRS. The median time to CRS onset was 1 day (range, 1–11), with a median duration of 6 days (range, 1–19). One patient in cohort 2 who had grade 2 CRS on days 6 to 11 also experienced grade 4 pericardial effusion on day 8 (duration, 2 days), which was deemed related to CRS caused by KITE-222 treatment. Two patients in cohort 3 had ICANS (one patient had grade 2; the other patient had grade 3 with subsequent CNS disease progression after 12 days). The median time to onset of ICANS was 4 days (range, 2–5), with a median duration of 4 days (range, 1–6).

All 12 patients died as of the data cutoff date. No deaths were considered related to KITE-222. Eleven patients died from disease progression. The one patient (cohort 3) who experienced a DLT died from sepsis on day 52 after infusion.

sec.title: Efficacy
sec.p: Of the 12 patients treated with KITE-222, one patient in cohort 3 achieved a best response of MLFS documented at day 14 after infusion and confirmed at days 27 and 44 (Fig. 2). This 61-year-old female patient, with adverse risk per ELN 2017 criteria based on ASXL1 mutations, was treated with KITE-222 cells at the target dose level for cohort 3 (3 × 108 cells) after two rounds of lymphodepletion (4,050 mg/m2 total cumulative cyclophosphamide received over the two rounds) separated by 17 days. Due to infection (concurrent with grade 4 cytopenias), the patient could not proceed to allo-HSCT despite achieving MLFS with KITE-222 and died on day 52.

sec.title: PK/PD
sec.p: Postinfusion expansion of KITE-222 cells, reported as CAR T cells/μL blood, was detected in 10 of 12 patients within 14 days after infusion (Fig. 3A). In cohorts 1 and 2, three patients had detectable KITE-222 cells at >1 time point (clear expansion), one patient had detectable KITE-222 cells only at a single time point (minimal expansion), and two patients did not have detectable KITE-222 cells at any time after infusion (no expansion). Median times to peak KITE-222 CAR T-cell levels were 11 days (range, 4–22) and 15 days (range, 3–15) for cohorts 1 and 2, respectively (Supplementary Table S7). In cohort 3, the five patients who received high-dose lymphodepletion had detectable KITE-222 cells within 7 days and at subsequent time points thereafter (clear expansion). In the only patient in cohort 3 who received low-dose cyclophosphamide, KITE-222 cells were detectable only at the 14-day time point (minimal expansion). The median time to KITE-222 cell peak in this cohort was 9 days (range, 8–15; Supplementary Table S7). At day 28, only 33% of the 12 treated patients had detectable KITE-222 cells in PB (one patient each in cohorts 1 and 2 and two patients in cohort 3; Fig. 3A). Median peak levels of KITE-222 cells in patients who received high- versus low-dose cyclophosphamide were 5.37 cells/μL (range, 0.90–79.17) and 1.65 cells/μL (range, 0–9.91), respectively (Supplementary Table S8); the difference was not significant by descriptive statistics (P = 0.1931). Median times to peak KITE-222 cells were 8 days (range, 8–11) and 15 days (range, 3–22) for patients who received high- versus low-dose cyclophosphamide, respectively (P = 0.2834). At day 28, two of five patients (40%) with expansion in each of the high- and low-dose cohorts had detectable KITE-222 cells (Fig. 3B).

sec.p: CAR T-cell detection, reported as CAR copies/μg DNA, is presented in Fig. 3C (by cohort) and Supplementary Fig. S2 (all cohorts); cohort 3 had an approximate 12- and 113-fold higher median peak vector copy number (VCN)/μg DNA compared with cohorts 1 and 2, respectively (Supplementary Table S7). In cohort 3, relatively high VCN/μg DNA was observed in three of five patients who received high-dose lymphodepletion, including the one patient who achieved MLFS and experienced a DLT following KITE-222 treatment.

KITE-222 CAR T-cell levels, measured either as cells/μL blood or VCN/μg DNA, were not associated with response nor with a clear reduction in AML disease burden. CLL-1+ blast percentages in BM per central assessment (flow cytometry) are shown in Fig. 4. Although there was near complete depletion of CLL-1+ BM blasts after KITE-222 infusion in two of five patients who had clear CAR T-cell expansion and also received high-dose LDC (cohort 3), reductions in total BM blasts were not observed due to the increasing proportions of CLL-1− blasts. The frequency of CLL-1+ blasts and overall blasts in PB over time also varied significantly, with patterns of total blast percentages and possible changes in CLL-1+ blast percentages that were inconsistent with patterns of CAR T-cell expansion (Supplementary Fig. S3). At baseline, all patients had ≥60% CLL-1+ blood monocytes, which did not seem to be eliminated by KITE-222 CAR T cells, as shown in Supplementary Fig. S4.

sec.p: Measurement of serum analytes following KITE-222 infusion showed that median postinfusion peak levels of homeostatic cytokines (IL2, IL7, and IL15) and chemokines (such as MCP-1 and CXCL-10) were increased at least 2-fold from baseline (Supplementary Table S9). Inflammatory and immune-modulating cytokines (IL1RA and GM-CSF in cohort 3 only, IFNγ and TNFα) and correlates of the acute phase response (C-reactive protein, ferritin, and serum amyloid A) were increased at least 4-fold from baseline.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In patients with R/R AML, rapid disease progression, nonhomogeneous and shifting target expression, and/or complications such as infections that lead to rapid clinical deterioration are challenges in the timely administration of CAR T-cell treatment (1, 8). Moreover, this instability in patient health contributes to a high attrition rate during the manufacturing waiting period for autologous cell therapy solutions. In fact, 20% of patients (3/15) enrolled in this study could not be treated with KITE-222 due to AML-related complications despite successful manufacturing of CAR T-cell products. High attrition of patients (20%–40%) has also been reported in other trials of autologous CAR T-cell therapy in AML (27, 28). The manufacturing of KITE-222 did not have a negative impact on timely infusion as products were released for infusion with a median time of 14 days for all 12 treated patients, and dosing was feasible even in two patients with out-of-specification products. Despite efficient manufacturing, a decline in patient health may have been a factor leading to the delayed initiation of LDC or CAR T-cell infusion in some patients.

In the primary endpoint analysis, 1 of 11 evaluable patients experienced a DLT of prolonged grade 4 cytopenias in the setting of AML remission. Other toxicities included ICANS and CRS, commonly associated with CAR T-cell therapies, which were manageable with no related DLTs. The patient in cohort 3 who experienced the DLT was also the only patient to achieve a best response of MLFS (on day 14) following KITE-222 infusion. This patient had peak CAR T-cell expansion on day 7, with detectable cells at day 42 and near-complete depletion of CLL-1+ BM blasts at day 14 following KITE-222 infusion, subsequent to two rounds of lymphodepletion. Despite achieving MLFS, the patient could not proceed to allo-HSCT and died of sepsis related to LDC on day 52. The high cumulative target dose of cyclophosphamide administered to this patient is a confounding factor in terms of expansion, achieving MLFS, and its contribution to toxicities associated with LDC that were likely additive.

In this study, clear in vivo expansion of KITE-222 CAR T cells was observed in 67% (8/12) of treated patients, albeit at highly variable levels. An LDC regimen consisting of cyclophosphamide and fludarabine is commonly used to enable adequate CAR T-cell expansion and enhance CAR T-cell function in patients with advanced non-Hodgkin lymphoma or B-cell malignancies (29–31). Among patients in dose-escalation cohorts 1 and 2, a cyclophosphamide dose of 300 mg/m2/day for 3 days was intended to support expansion while minimizing the duration of hematopoietic recovery. However, initial translational findings from these cohorts suggested a possible inverse relationship between tumor burden and CAR T-cell expansion (not shown). To enable better CAR T-cell expansion, reduce nonleukemic CLL-1+ cells, and promote engagement of the CAR with CLL-1+ target cells, LDC enhancement with cyclophosphamide 750 mg/m2/day for 3 days was evaluated in 5 of 6 patients in cohort 3. This adjustment was based on previous experiences suggesting that such enhanced lymphodepletion via high-dose cyclophosphamide may improve response by promoting a favorable cytokine profile, reducing the suppression of CAR T-cell function, and/or increasing CAR T-cell survival (32, 33). CAR T-cell expansion was observed in all five of these patients at highly variable levels, suggesting a likely positive contribution of high-dose LDC to CAR T-cell expansion. However, due to the relatively small sample size of the study and the potential for increased toxicity, this conjecture requires further investigation. When compared with the degree of expansion reported for well-characterized CD19-targeting CAR T-cell products, peak expansion of KITE-222 CAR T cells appeared relatively low in all but one patient despite the abundant presence of antigen (24, 31, 34, 35). For instance, in the ZUMA-2 and ZUMA-3 trials of brexu-cel and the ZUMA-1 and ZUMA-5 trials of axi-cel, the median peak CAR T cells/μL blood were 88.64, 20.62, 38.25, and 39.38, respectively (24, 31, 34, 35). The lack of preliminary clinical response in all cohorts together with the lack of clear and consistent depletion of CLL-1+ blasts, even in the presence of detectable CAR T-cell expansion, indicates that there are additional barriers to efficacy with CAR T cells in AML, aside from the optimization of CAR T-cell expansion and persistence (36, 37). Furthermore, due to the lack of efficacy, the contribution of AML-associated genetic abnormalities to patient outcomes could not be assessed.

AML disease heterogeneity as a possible mechanism of resistance was consistent with the nearly complete depletion of CLL-1+ BM blasts at day 14 observed in two of five patients who had clear CAR T-cell expansion (cohort 3) without an associated reduction in total BM blasts. This finding could be due to an abundance of CLL-1− blasts either present at baseline or emergent during therapy or other mechanisms of antigen escape such as shedding, genetic alterations, and transcriptional downregulation, which have been observed in the context of CD19-directed CAR T-cell therapy in B-cell malignancies (38). A dual (or even triple)-targeting CAR construct (e.g., CLL-1/CD33 dual CAR) may possibly overcome these issues and improve efficacy (18, 39). Beyond target heterogeneity in AML, recent articles have highlighted the role of cytokines in mechanisms of resistance to T-cell–based immunotherapies in AML (28, 40). Findings from a study of an autologous CD123-targeted CAR T-cell therapy in AML provided evidence of a novel mechanism of CAR T-cell exhaustion unique to AML (28). The myeloid-supporting cytokines (e.g., GM-CSF and IL3) secreted during cell therapy were shown to promote AML survival and antigen persistence, leading to CAR T-cell exhaustion. Consistent with these observations, we found that patients in cohort 3 had elevated GM-CSF levels compared with cohorts 1 and 2, which may have supported AML resistance to KITE-222 therapy despite some levels of CAR T-cell expansion in all six patients. Cohort 3 GM-CSF levels also appeared elevated compared with postinfusion peak levels previously observed in patients with B-cell malignancies treated with the CD19-targeting CAR T cells axicabtagene ciloleucel or brexucabtagene autoleucel (24, 31, 34). Another study investigating SOCS1, a protein associated with high-risk AML mutations, suggested that SOCS1 overexpression could create resistance to the action of IFNγ by affecting the immune synapse of ICAM-1 and LFA-1 (40). The lack of antitumor effects observed in these studies may be attributable, in part, to impaired CAR T-cell function arising from exhaustion or impairment in immune synapse formation. In this regard, a pilot study of anti–CLL-1 CAR T cells armored with IL18 has shown promise, with potential improvements in in vivo expansion and leukemic cell clearance in heavily pretreated patients with R/R AML (41).

The lack of a suitable surface antigen, homogeneously expressed in the majority of AML blasts and exclusive to AML cells, remains a key challenge in developing CAR T-cell therapy and, in general, immune-harnessing therapies for AML (1, 42). Unlike other target antigens such as CD123 and CD33, CLL-1 expression is minimal or absent in normal HSPCs or nonhematopoietic cells, reducing the risk of on-target/off-tumor toxicities, including prolonged myelosuppression (1, 15, 22, 43). However, CLL-1 expression can be dynamic, and fluctuations are observed in AML, with a wide range of expression on blasts. CLL-1 is expressed in 70% to 87% of CD34+CD38− AML blasts and is also present on CD34+CD38− leukemic stem cells, which can be difficult to target because of their ability to acquire quiescence and confer chemotherapy resistance, possibly resulting in relapse (43–46). About 25% of patients with AML have bimodal CLL-1 expression marked by positive/high expression and negative/low expression on two distinct blast subsets (46). This bimodal expression pattern, likely resulting from the heterogeneous nature of AML, may pose challenges for CLL-1–directed therapies (46). Only 64% of treated patients with available CLL-1 expression data at baseline presented with >20% CLL-1+ BM blasts, potentially compromising the ability of KITE-222 to effectively eradicate the disease.

Several drugs targeting CLL-1 have been investigated in AML, including antibody–drug conjugates, bispecific antibodies, and CAR T-cell therapies (18, 47, 48). In a phase 1 trial of a CLL-1–targeted antibody–drug conjugate in adult patients with AML, no DLTs were reported throughout the 21-day assessment period, but dose escalation was terminated due to safety concerns and lack of antileukemic activity (47). Other trials investigating various constructs of autologous CLL-1–directed CAR T cells in AML have reported promising results; however, these studies were largely focused on pediatric patients with AML, and only short-term outcomes in small numbers of patients have thus far been reported (8, 49–52). Long-term disease control and survival, dose–response correlations, limited sample sizes, and variability in the conduct and reporting of CAR T-cell trials in AML are ongoing challenges (52, 53).

Due to the lack of formal ELN remissions with KITE-222, the study was closed after the dose-escalation phase. The expansion phase was not initiated, and the development of KITE-222 has been discontinued. In addition to the suboptimal expansion of KITE-222 (especially with standard-dose LDC and at lower CAR T-cell doses), other factors may account for the lack of an efficacy signal in this trial, including CAR T-cell exhaustion, CLL-1 antigen escape, increased myeloid-specific cytokines promoting AML growth, and a possible immunosuppressive leukemic microenvironment (18, 28, 39). Additionally, the T-cell fitness of the autologous material used for CAR T-cell manufacturing may have been relatively suboptimal in some patients given that they were heavily pretreated. Although we do not have the data to support the enrichment of regulatory, suppressive, or exhausted T cells in the chronic environment of the tumor associated with multiple lines of prior therapy, reduced T-cell fitness may have influenced KITE-222 potency (54–57). Future studies of novel autologous CAR T-cell products for AML, which focus on improved T-cell function and simultaneous targeting of more than one antigen to mitigate antigen escape, are warranted and should include less heavily treated patients and ideally dedicated cohorts for those with lower tumor burden (including patients in remission with detectable minimal residual disease). Additionally, the investigation of costimulatory/coinhibitory molecules that affect T-cell activation, expansion, and persistence, specifically in AML, is also needed.

In summary, KITE-222, a CLL-1–directed CAR T-cell therapy, was ineffective in treating adult patients with R/R AML. Responses were lacking despite the successful manufacturing of CAR T-cell products for all patients. KITE-222 CAR T-cell expansion was absent or minimal in 33% of patients and was highly variable in the remaining patients, with an observed improvement in the expansion and persistence of CAR T cells following enhanced lymphodepletion dosing in patients who received the highest dose level of KITE-222. Further modifications and enhancements, as discussed here, may help improve the efficacy and eventual successful implementation of CAR T-cell therapy in AML.
